Name: Lightyear
Review:
This wasn’t a bad movie by any chance, and my rating says that, but it still disappointed me because of where it’s coming from. Pixar saw an opportunity to make money and they took it, and while Lightyear was better than I thought it would be, it was still low Pixar. It was an undercooked, cookie-cutter rendition of the classic old school sci-fi genre, and while I understand that the creators didn’t want to deviate away from that, they just missed the mark in the process.

Lightyear isn’t one of Pixar’s more philosophical works, and as far as classic sci-fi goes, it doesn’t want to reinvent the wheel either, both of which I respect. But the result is a classic sci-fi that pretends to have heart but doesn’t because it lacks a strong enough base. Lightyear builds itself on a weak foundation of underdeveloped relationships and takes focus away from characters that could have made the story easier to resonate with. The audience is expected to care about the junior squad but what do we know about them anyway, besides them being comic relief? We are expected to care about Alicia but apart from her being commander hawthorn’s grandkid, we don’t know much about her either. These characters are based around buzz, to support his story, which is the worst way to build characters. But even if we run with that, our titular character is nothing more than a shell of a classic male protagonist with a hero complex. Nothing wrong with any of those things individually, if you let the audience get to know him and let them connect. But lightyear leaves all of that to focus on the plot instead.

Where the characters are underdeveloped, the plot is overcooked. The thing that made classic sci-fi movies good was the simplicity (which is how they focussed on characters and developed heart), but lightyear tries to do too much—with one objective for the characters and too many hurdles along the way. This means that the characters have no room to breath, and when there’s no room to breathe, you can’t really build an emotional core. When buzz does finally meet Zurg, and it turns out to be alt old buzz, it seems more like a gimmick more than anything. The antagonist is really not that antagonizing anymore, because given Zurg’s experiences, his opinions make perfect sense. Zurg was never evil, but the script somehow turned his very rational motivations into disproportionately large actions, none of which made sense. Where I would have expected redemption for such a misguided character, especially in a movie made for children, he is defeated by our ‘hero’.

While the visuals are cool, and the facial expressions are very well done, this movie did not need animation as it’s form. Obviously if Pixar wants to make a lightyear film, it needs to be animated, but in its current form the creators are doing nothing that cannot be achieved with a live action film with cgi and practical effects. When put next to Soul or Turning red, which required animation for what they were trying to say, lightyear simply falls short. There’s no concept here that has come directly from a creators imagination to the screen, and that’s what animation exists for.

I’m not disappointed because my expectations weren’t that high, I’m just confused. If this movie was bad, I would have nothing to say, but it’s almost good, and that’s annoying. The Pixar of my childhood was never philosophical, but rats who cook and talking cars and toys coming to life were things all so magical and heartfelt that you connected instantly. These things could never be shown in live action. They never reinvented the wheel, they had a strong emotional core, and it was authentic. They never tried to be emotional because they felt like they had to. Pixar used to be consistent, but now, Pixar movies are a hit or miss, and when it’s a miss, it often feels like Pixar is just trying to imitate themselves.

Name: Oppenheimer
Review: When artists indulge, they end up making this brain-foggy scribble monster of ideas. A piece of living, breathing, highly imperfect art whose unyielding ebbs and flows form an almost humanistic emotional shape, each piece of the jigsaw existing in a superposition of meaning, contradicting and colliding with one another. It’s existence forms a paradox, and it thrives in self disagreement. These waves of vibrant diverse colors overlap as they exist in a state of constant motion and fluidity, moving into and out of each other to give form to the new. They end up resting on top of one another like many celluloid frames to produce a plain solidity and shrouded in it, mystery - intricacies and complexity. In its creation there is a kind of unfiltered childish haphazardness, no clear bold stream of ideas, no clear objective or priorities or decisions. This is what it means for it to be living almost humanistically, it itself does not know anything about the ideas behind its creation and conception and existence and it doesn’t even want to, it basks in the shine and rests in the shadow of its own glory like people do. Oppenheimer feels human because it embodies its central character in a sense so complete that it begs the question if it was an happy accident. In an attempt at giving you a look into the character’s mind, it might’ve slipped and gotten locked in a room inside it. Forever festering in that environment, taking the viewer into a level of immersion unseen. Oppenheimer does not make you feel like you know the man, in fact you’d feel alienated, even after 3 hours with him you probably won’t be able to hold a conversation with him, rather it makes you feel like you are him.  As you take the spot marked Oppenheimer, you become him completely, and probably not much differently to how you yourself feel in life, you have no idea who you are. You haven’t the slightest idea of what people see when they look at you, good or bad. Like in real life, you only know your own thoughts, you are imprisoned in them. Perhaps there’s a certain kind of dark cloud before your eyes, which fades away to give way to pristine clarity when you close your eyes. And in this ever so universal paradoxical state of clarity and confusion, you are given the choice. Do you do it? You’d be the man who moved the earth. You could play God. You’d be able to change the world, do something so big and unfathomable that things dwarf in its presence. Something to tie yourself to, so that you yourself don’t float away in the vast space of life. You fear it though. You don’t fear the fire itself, rather the thought of the bomb's absolute and immense destruction swallowing the earth, swallows your mind. Even your fear centers around the role you played in creating it. Perhaps you love the guilt because it means you mean something. Perhaps to you it's not truly about whether what you did was right or wrong, but that it was "worthy" of such a debate. That at the very least, whether they keep punishing you or forgive you and whether you die a hero, genius, martyr, or death itself, at least everyone will remember.

Name: Raging Bull
Review:
I like marty, unlike what most of my ratings will have you believe, and as I watch more of his work I feel like i’m starting to understand what he’s trying to say a little better. He is, for the lack of better words, the incel’s filmmaker. Almost every film he makes, he forces you to take a look directly in the eye of morality and makes you aware of the evil within yourself. The bum in you that has anger and resentment and jealousy and bitterness towards the world, verging on evil. He doesn’t judge you for it though, it’s only fair since most men have that in them somewhere. Call it the curse of masculinity. He doesn’t judge you for it because he recognizes how these things come from a place of loneliness and isolation. But it’s almost like he’s expecting that you’ll judge yourself for it because you know that there’s no excuse for being this belligerent. He seems to be only propping up a mirror. It almost seems like he’s convinced men can’t change and this is just how it is. His lack of hope/empathy doesn’t sit right with me. I like to think your inner morality is strong enough to recognize why some things are objectively immoral, and you’re able to get over your primal instincts to become someone you’d actually like. The issue is, his lack of explicit judgement results in an uncomfortable number of us who watch one of his movies and reflexively utter the words ‘that was so fucking cool’. I understand that’s instinctive - when I watch his movies and start to connect with the main character, the parts of me brewed over years of toxic masculinity feel seen - but before I can say the word ‘cool’ atleast there forms in me a lump of self hate and a need to do better. He’s still not my dude, and on a personal preference level, his work is a little less juicy than I’d like, but atleast i’m starting to get him. P.S. a review I liked on here:
my favourite thing about Marty is that he will never make me feel bad or icky about liking or disliking a character in his movies. he understands men and is unafraid to brutally strip them naked & brandish all the lies they tell us. my favourite thing about Marty is that no matter the subject of his films, I can still sit through and watch them, and not be disappointed. if you are a man and you find yourself rooting for one of his male characters, catch yourself being joyous at their rise, then take a hard look at yourself in the mirror. because if you are a man who is eager to like the men in his films, you will be disappointed. and you will be a disappointment to the world.
